name: Coaching Students Through Primary Sources
title: Coaching Students Through Primary Sources

crumbs.name: Social Studies, Civics, and World Languages

reading.body:
A school configured AI tool can coach students through primary sources by asking the questions a historian would ask, without interpreting the documents for them.

The pattern is a division of labor. The tool supplies questions, such as who created the document, when, what the author was trying to accomplish, what it leaves out, and who might see it differently. The student supplies the answers, the reading, the reasoning, and the writing. The tool asks follow up questions but does not say what the source means.

This matters for AI because it is a case where the model's output is not the product. In document based questions the teacher can configure a hint only tool that helps a student plan an essay across a set of documents without writing it, asking which documents support the argument and which complicate it. The scarce resource in that exchange is not generated text but the student's own judgment, and the tool is arranged so it cannot substitute for it.

The guardrails are where the limits show. Teachers choose the sources, because AI tools sometimes describe documents that do not exist or misquote real ones, so every source should come from an archive, a library database, or a trusted collection. The text gives no study, figure, or finding for this idea and rests on practice rather than research, and it does not give grade band variations. What the data does not cover is whether the approach improves student work, and it says nothing about the compute, buildings, or power behind the tool.

sections.body: Primary sources such as letters, speeches, photographs, and government records are the raw material of history, and reading them well is a skill built over years. Large collections are available free from the Library of Congress and many state archives. AI can help students work with these sources without doing the interpreting for them. A school configured tool acts as a coach, asking the questions a historian would ask, such as who created the document and when, what the author was trying to accomplish, what it leaves out, and who might see it differently. The student answers and the coach asks follow up questions, but the tool does not tell the student what the source means.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: Document based questions work well with this approach. A teacher can set up a hint only tool, as described in Chapter 7, that helps students plan an essay using a set of documents without writing the essay. The tool might ask which documents support the student's argument and which complicate it. The student does the reading, the reasoning, and the writing. The text does not give grade band variations for this idea.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text gives no study, figure, or finding for this idea. It rests on practice rather than research.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: Teachers should choose the sources themselves. AI tools can suggest documents, but they sometimes describe documents that do not exist or misquote real ones. Every source students use should come from an archive, a library database, or a trusted collection. The coach helps students read real sources, not invented ones. The decisions about which sources to use and what they mean stay with the teacher and the student.
